read the junior encyclopaedia to obtain information for lifelong learning

skills.name: Use a dictionary: order, guide words and meaning
skills.mastery: Puts words in alphabetical order (using the second and third letters when the first match), uses guide words to find the page, and picks the right meaning of a word from its entry, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Choose the right reference book
skills.mastery: Chooses the dictionary, junior encyclopaedia, atlas, newspaper or timetable for what the child needs to find out, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Orders words by the first letter only.
misconceptions.cause: Stops comparing after the first letter.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Order: bat, bag, ball" with "bat, bag, ball" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "bag, ball, bat", not "bat, bag, ball".
misconceptions.feedback: When the first letters match, look at the second letter, then the third.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not use the guide words to find the page.

example.question: Guide words "cat" and "cow": is "cup" on this page?

misconceptions.cause: Does not know guide words are the first and last words on the page.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Guide words "cat" and "cow": is "cup" on this page?" with "Yes" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "No", not "Yes".
misconceptions.feedback: Guide words show the first and last words on a page. A word is on the page only if it comes between them in alphabetical order.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a meaning that fits another sense of the word.

example.question: sprint
example.correct_answer: a very fast run for a short distance

misconceptions.cause: Chooses the first meaning that sounds familiar.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "sprint" with "a long walk" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "a very fast run for a short distance", not "a long walk".
misconceptions.feedback: Read all the meanings, then try each in the sentence to see which one fits.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a dictionary to find facts about a topic.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks every reference book does the same job.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "You want facts about elephants." with "a dictionary" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "a junior encyclopaedia", not "a dictionary".
misconceptions.feedback: A dictionary tells the meaning and spelling of words. A junior encyclopaedia gives facts about topics.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses an atlas to find the meaning of a word.

example.question: You want to find a map of Kenya.

misconceptions.cause: Does not link the book to what it holds.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "You want to find a map of Kenya." with "a dictionary" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "an atlas", not "a dictionary".
misconceptions.feedback: An atlas is a book of maps. Use it to find places and countries.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a story book to look up information.

example.question: You want to know a bus time.

misconceptions.cause: Thinks a book is good for any need.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "You want to know a bus time." with "a story book" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "a timetable", not "a story book".
misconceptions.feedback: A timetable lists times. A story book tells an invented story and is not for looking things up.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a newspaper for facts that do not change.
misconceptions.cause: Does not think about when the information is needed.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "You want today's news." with "a dictionary" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "a newspaper", not "a dictionary".
misconceptions.feedback: A newspaper gives news of today. A dictionary or encyclopaedia gives facts that stay the same.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

learning_experiences: read aloud the articles a, an and the with peers,
identify definite and indefinite articles (a, an, and the) from a paragraph,
collaborate to match definite and indefinite articles with a list of nouns,
complete blanks in sentences using correct articles,
construct sentences with peers using definite and indefinite articles,
type sentences on a digital device and share with friends or family via mobile phone, email, computer printouts, among others,
view a video related to the theme in which the definite and indefinite articles are used,
cooperate with others to search for sentences with articles from a selected newspaper, magazine or internet.
key_inquiry_questions: How are articles used with nouns?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and Imagination: This is developed as the learner creates sentences containing articles and shares the content via digital device.
Critical thinking and problem solving: This is promoted as the learner completes blanks in sentences using correct articles.
sub_strands.values:
Tolerance: This is developed as the learner is able to accommodate diverse views from peers when searching for sentences with articles from a selected newspaper, magazine or internet.
Love: It is cultivated as the learner is able to show empathy and take initiative to assist others as they use technology to share their work.
sub_strands.pcis: Digital Safety: This is promoted as the learner observes discipline and cyber safety as they share their work through mobile phones, emails or online platforms.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the concept of definite and indefinite articles to their learning of similar concepts in Foreign Langauges.

outcomes.text: identify definite and indefinite articles in a written text for effective communication
use definite and indefinite articles in sentences for effective communication
acknowledge the use of articles in oral and written contexts for self-expression

skills.name: Use a, an and the
skills.mastery: Chooses or writes a, an or the (a before a consonant sound, an before a vowel sound, the for a known or named thing, no article for things in general) and finds the one wrong article in a short note, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Writes a before a word that starts with a vowel sound.
misconceptions.cause: Learns "a" as the only small word and does not listen to the first sound of the next word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "She ate ___ orange." with "a" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "an", not "a".
misconceptions.feedback: Before a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u) use "an": an orange, an egg.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes an before a word that starts with a consonant sound.
misconceptions.cause: Over-corrects after learning that "an" goes before vowels.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I bought ___ book." with "an" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "a", not "an".
misconceptions.feedback: Before a consonant sound use "a": a book, a pen.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a or an by the first letter, not the first sound.
misconceptions.cause: Looks at the letter h (or u) instead of listening to the sound.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "We waited for ___ hour." with "a" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "an", not "a".
misconceptions.feedback: Listen to the sound, not the letter. "Hour" starts with the sound "ow", so it takes "an". "Uniform" starts with the sound "yoo", so it takes "a".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the for something that has not been mentioned before.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks the is the main article.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Mama gave me ___ apple." with "the" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "an", not "the".
misconceptions.feedback: Use a or an the first time you speak about a thing. Use the when both people already know which one.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a or an for something that is known or the only one.

example.question: We feel the heat of ___ sun.

misconceptions.cause: Does not see that there is only one of it.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "We feel the heat of ___ sun." with "a" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "the", not "a".
misconceptions.feedback: Use the for something that is the only one (the sun, the moon) or that both people know about.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the article before a singular noun.
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili has no articles, so the small word is not heard as needed.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Kamau has ___ new bicycle." with "no article" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "a", not "no article".
misconceptions.feedback: A singular thing you can count needs a, an or the before it: a new bicycle.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses the for things in general, or uses a with a plural.
misconceptions.cause: Believes "the" is needed before every noun.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "___ lions are strong animals." with "The" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "no article (Lions are strong animals.)", not "The".
misconceptions.feedback: When you speak about a kind of thing in general, use no article: Lions are strong animals. Use "the" for one particular thing both people know.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

learning_experiences: fill forms provided by the teacher with specific details such as: Personal details Name ______ Grade _______ Date of Birth _________ School Details Name _______ Address ______ Name of Class Teacher _______ Name of Head teacher ________,
read instructions on filling in forms collaboratively,
record the required information related to the theme in the forms with peers,
team up to fill in forms in print format and display them,
download online forms and fill in information with guidance from the teacher,
create a form, and type it on a computer, laptop or tablet.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should one be careful when filling in forms?
What information do we fill in forms?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and Imagination: This is promoted as the learner generates ideas and uses them to create a form and shares it with peers.
Digital Literacy: It is enhanced as the learner manipulates digital devices to download, create and fill in forms.
sub_strands.values:
Love: This is promoted as the learner accommodates other’s contributions as they work jointly to fill in forms.
Integrity : This is promoted as the learner willingly displays their forms for peer review and feedback.
sub_strands.pcis: Gender Education: This is promoted as the learner interacts with content about the various people and genders in the theme of family.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the concept of filling in forms to their learning in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify the required information to be filled in forms for different purposes
fill information in forms correctly for self-expression
realise the importance of filling forms correctly for effective communication

skills.name: Know what goes in each part of a form
skills.mastery: Says which piece of information belongs in a box of a school, clinic or library form (name, date of birth, class, address, parent contact), in 8 of 10 new items.

misconceptions.error: Writes the wrong detail in a box.
misconceptions.cause: Does not read what the box asks for.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Date of birth: " with "Nairobi" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "14th March 2016", not "Nairobi".
misconceptions.feedback: Read the name of the box first, then write only what it asks for.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the age in the date of birth box.
misconceptions.cause: Confuses age with date of birth.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Date of birth: " with "9 years" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "14th March 2016", not "9 years".
misconceptions.feedback: Date of birth needs the day, month and year you were born. Age is a number.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes a phone number in the address box.
misconceptions.cause: Does not tell address from contact.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Home address: " with "0712 345 678" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "P.O. Box 12, Kisumu", not "0712 345 678".
misconceptions.feedback: An address says where you live or get letters. A phone number goes in the contact box.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes only one name in the full names box.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks the first name is enough.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Full names: " with "Wanjiru" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Wanjiru Kamau Njeri", not "Wanjiru".
misconceptions.feedback: Full names means all of your names, in the order the form asks for.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

Which words are used as subjects in a sentence?
sub_strands.core_competences:

sub_strands.values:
Unity: This is enhanced as the learner cooperates with peers to use word wheels to form new words with target sounds.
Love: It is developed as the learner displays an attitude of care for others as they work together.

sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the concept of pronunciation to their learning in Kiswahili.

read a poem or story (featuring similes and sayings) in print and non-print texts related to the theme for comprehension,

What is your favourite poem or story?

Social justice: This is promoted as the learner fosters fairness by allowing equal opportunities to peers when participating in a readers' theatre.
Responsibility: This is enhanced as the learner engages in assigned roles and duties diligently.

skills.name: Answer direct questions from a text
skills.mastery: Finds an answer that is written in the text (who, what, where, when) and says whether a statement is true, false or not stated, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Answer indirect questions from a text
skills.mastery: Works out what is not written but is shown by clues (why a person felt or did something) and does not copy a sentence, go against the text or go too far, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose what can be worked out

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use clues in the text to find a word's meaning
skills.mastery: Picks the meaning of a new word from the sentences around it, and the words that give the clue, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Picks a detail that sits near the answer in the text.

example.question: What was tied inside the bag?

misconceptions.cause: Reads fast and picks a nearby word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "What was tied inside the bag?" with "sand" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "rags", not "sand".
misconceptions.feedback: Find the sentence that answers the question and check that the words match what is asked.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Answers from what he or she already knows.
misconceptions.cause: Does not go back to the text.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "How did they travel?" with "by bus" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "by boda boda", not "by bus".
misconceptions.feedback: Answer from the text, not from what you think is likely. Go back to the sentence.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says not stated when the text does say it.

example.question: True, false or not stated: Achieng set tomatoes in heaps.

misconceptions.cause: Does not find the sentence.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "True, false or not stated: Achieng set tomatoes in heaps." with "Not stated" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "True", not "Not stated".
misconceptions.feedback: Look again. When the text says it clearly, the answer is true.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says true when the text says something different.
misconceptions.cause: Reads for the topic, not the exact detail.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The market was in Nakuru." with "True" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "False", not "True".
misconceptions.feedback: The text says something different from the statement, so the statement is false.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says not stated when the text says something different.
misconceptions.cause: Does not tell going against the text from saying nothing.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The market was in Nakuru." with "Not stated" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "False", not "Not stated".
misconceptions.feedback: If the text says the opposite, the answer is false. Not stated means the text says nothing about it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says true or false when the text does not say.
misconceptions.cause: Fills in what seems likely.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Kamau scored a goal." with "True" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Not stated", not "True".
misconceptions.feedback: The text does not mention it, so the answer is not stated. Do not guess from what is likely.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks the wrong person or place for who or where.
misconceptions.cause: Picks the first name seen.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Who helped Kamau?" with "his teacher" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "his grandmother", not "his teacher".
misconceptions.feedback: Find the sentence about the helper and check who it names.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Copies a sentence from the text as the answer.

example.question: Why did Mother nod proudly?
example.wrong_answer: The woman wore a green dress.
example.correct_answer: Achieng counted carefully and gave the right change.

misconceptions.cause: Does not see that the answer is not written.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Why did Mother nod proudly?" with "The woman wore a green dress." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Achieng counted carefully and gave the right change.", not "The woman wore a green dress.".
misconceptions.feedback: An inference is worked out from clues. A sentence copied from the text is not working anything out.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks an answer that goes against the text.

example.question: Why was Kamau sad?
example.correct_answer: He loved football and the ball burst.

misconceptions.cause: Does not check the answer against the text.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Why was Kamau sad?" with "The school was closed." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "He loved football and the ball burst.", not "The school was closed.".
misconceptions.feedback: A good inference agrees with every clue in the text.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks an answer that goes too far.

example.question: What can you tell about the grandmother?
example.wrong_answer: She is the richest woman in town.

misconceptions.cause: Adds facts that the text does not support.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "What can you tell about the grandmother?" with "She is the richest woman in town." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "She is kind and clever.", not "She is the richest woman in town.".
misconceptions.feedback: An inference is a small step from the clues. If the text gives no clue for it, it goes too far.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a meaning that looks like the word.
misconceptions.cause: Guesses from the look of the word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "burst" with "rolled away" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "broke open", not "rolled away".
misconceptions.feedback: Read the sentences around the word to find its meaning.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a common meaning that does not fit.
misconceptions.cause: Uses a known meaning without testing it.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "heaps" with "big baskets" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "small piles", not "big baskets".
misconceptions.feedback: Try the meaning in the sentence. If it does not fit, it is not the right one.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks the opposite meaning.
misconceptions.cause: Does not read the clue.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "ancient" with "very new" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "very old", not "very new".
misconceptions.feedback: Read for clue words. They tell you if the word means the same as or the opposite of something.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a group of words that does not explain the word.

example.question: Which words help you?
example.correct_answer: the school had no money for a new one

misconceptions.cause: Picks any phrase near the word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which words help you?" with "in Nyeri" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "the school had no money for a new one", not "in Nyeri".
misconceptions.feedback: A clue is a group of words that tells more about the hard word, not just words near it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Make regular plurals
skills.mastery: Forms the plural of regular nouns (-s, -es after s, x, ch, sh, -ies after a consonant and y, -ves for knife and leaf) and does not add -s to a number-plus-noun that is already plural, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Make irregular plurals
skills.mastery: Writes the plural of man, woman, child, foot, tooth, mouse, person, sheep and fish and does not add -s or a second plural ending, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Adds only -s to a word that ends in s, x, ch or sh.
misconceptions.cause: Uses the plain -s rule for every word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "two ___ (box)" with "boxs" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "boxes", not "boxs".
misconceptions.feedback: After s, x, ch and sh we add -es so that the word can be said: box, boxes; church, churches.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to a word that ends in a consonant and y.
misconceptions.cause: Does not change y to i before the ending.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "three ___ (baby)" with "babys" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "babies", not "babys".
misconceptions.feedback: When a word ends in a consonant and y, change the y to i and add -es: baby, babies.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Changes y to -ies after a vowel.
misconceptions.cause: Over-corrects after learning baby, babies.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "two ___ (monkey)" with "monkies" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "monkeys", not "monkies".
misconceptions.feedback: When a vowel comes before the y, just add -s: monkey, monkeys; day, days.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to knife, leaf, wife and loaf.
misconceptions.cause: Does not know the f to v change.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "two ___ (leaf)" with "leafs" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "leaves", not "leafs".
misconceptions.feedback: Some words ending in f or fe change to -ves: leaf, leaves; knife, knives; wife, wives.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Keeps the noun singular after a number.
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili does not change the noun after a number in the same way.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I have four ___." with "book" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "books", not "book".
misconceptions.feedback: After two, three, four or any number above one, the noun must be plural: four books.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to an irregular noun.
misconceptions.cause: Uses the regular rule for every noun.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "three ___ (child)" with "childs" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "children", not "childs".
misconceptions.feedback: A few nouns change in their own way. The plural of child is children, and of man is men.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to a plural that is already plural.
misconceptions.cause: Knows the word changes but adds -s from habit.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Many ___ were playing. (child)" with "childrens" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "children", not "childrens".
misconceptions.feedback: Children, men and women are already plural. Do not add -s.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes tooths, mouses or gooses.
misconceptions.cause: Does not know the vowel change.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "two ___ (tooth)" with "tooths" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "teeth", not "tooths".
misconceptions.feedback: Some plurals change the vowels inside the word: tooth, teeth; mouse, mice; goose, geese.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to sheep or fish.
misconceptions.cause: Treats every animal word as regular.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "ten ___ (sheep)" with "sheeps" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "sheep", not "sheeps".
misconceptions.feedback: Sheep stays sheep. We say one sheep and ten sheep. Fish is the same.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Choose polite words and phrases
skills.mastery: Picks the polite word or phrase for a situation (asking, thanking, apologising, refusing) and does not choose a command or a rude answer, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Makes a request as a demand.

example.question: You want to borrow a pen. What do you say?
example.correct_answer: May I please borrow your pen?

misconceptions.cause: Says the shortest thing that gets the pen.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "You want to borrow a pen. What do you say?" with "Give me your pen." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "May I please borrow your pen?", not "Give me your pen.".
misconceptions.feedback: A polite request starts with May I or Could you, and says please.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not say thank you.

example.question: Your friend helps you. What do you say?

misconceptions.cause: Does not see thanks as needed.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Your friend helps you. What do you say?" with "Okay." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Thank you for helping me.", not "Okay.".
misconceptions.feedback: When someone helps you, say thank you.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Refuses in a rude way.

example.question: You cannot lend your book. What do you say?
example.correct_answer: I am sorry, I cannot lend it today.

misconceptions.cause: Does not know how to say no politely.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "You cannot lend your book. What do you say?" with "No. Go away." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "I am sorry, I cannot lend it today.", not "No. Go away.".
misconceptions.feedback: You can say no in a polite way: begin with I am sorry.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not say sorry after a mistake.

example.question: You step on someone's foot. What do you say?
example.correct_answer: Sorry, I did not see you.

misconceptions.cause: Does not see that sorry is needed.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "You step on someone's foot. What do you say?" with "Move." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Sorry, I did not see you.", not "Move.".
misconceptions.feedback: When you hurt or bother someone, say sorry.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use May I, Could you and Would you like
skills.mastery: Builds and recognises polite requests and offers (May I go out, please? Could you help me? Would you like some tea?) with the plain verb after May I and Could you, in whole sentences, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Puts to, -s or -ing after May I or Could you.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks every verb needs "to" before it.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "May I ___ in?" with "to come" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "come", not "to come".
misconceptions.feedback: After May I and Could you the verb stays plain: May I come in? Could you help me?
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Makes a request as a command.

example.question: Which is polite? Give me water.
example.correct_answer: Could you give me some water, please?

misconceptions.cause: Uses the command that is quick and short.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is polite? Give me water." with "Give me water." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Could you give me some water, please?", not "Give me water.".
misconceptions.feedback: A polite request uses May I or Could you, and the word please.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes Would you like with -ing or a wrong verb form.
misconceptions.cause: Mixes Would you like with Do you want.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "___ you like some tea?" with "Do" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Would", not "Do".
misconceptions.feedback: To offer something politely we say: Would you like some tea? The verb after like is to + the plain verb, or a noun.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the words of the request in the wrong order.
misconceptions.cause: Does not move the helping word before the subject.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Could ___ help me?" with "help you" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "you help", not "help you".
misconceptions.feedback: In a request the helping word comes first: Could you help me? May I borrow your pen?
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use first aid words
skills.mastery: Uses the words of first aid (bandage, wound, bruise, sprain, ambulance, first aid kit) in the right sentence, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Picks a first aid word that is near in meaning but wrong.

example.question: A ___ is a cloth wrapped round a cut.

misconceptions.cause: Mixes up words in the same topic.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "A ___ is a cloth wrapped round a cut." with "bruise" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "bandage", not "bruise".
misconceptions.feedback: Read the whole sentence and say what the gap must mean before choosing.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up wound and bruise.

example.question: A ___ is a dark mark on the skin where you were hit.

misconceptions.cause: Treats the two words as the same.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "A ___ is a dark mark on the skin where you were hit." with "wound" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "bruise", not "wound".
misconceptions.feedback: A wound is a cut or a break in the skin. A bruise is a dark mark under the skin.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up sprain and break.

example.question: When you twist your ankle, it may be a ___.

misconceptions.cause: Does not know the words.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "When you twist your ankle, it may be a ___." with "ambulance" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "sprain", not "ambulance".
misconceptions.feedback: A sprain is a twisted joint. An ambulance is a vehicle that takes people to hospital.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads the wrong row or column of a table.

example.question: What time does the bus to Kisumu leave?

misconceptions.cause: Looks at the nearest number instead of the row for Kisumu.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "What time does the bus to Kisumu leave?" with "10:30 am" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "8:00 am", not "10:30 am".

misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says the wrong purpose for a visual.

misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use I, me, he, him, we, us, they and them
skills.mastery: Chooses the subject form before the verb and the object form after the verb or a small word, and does not repeat a noun with a pronoun (Wanjiru she is tall), in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use mine, yours, hers, ours and theirs
skills.mastery: Writes mine, yours, his, hers, ours or theirs when no noun follows, my, your, her, our or their before a noun, and never writes your's, her's or our's, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses I, he, we or they after a verb or a small word.
misconceptions.cause: Hears "Him and I" in speech and over-corrects.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Mum gave the book to ___." with "I" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "me", not "I".
misconceptions.feedback: After a verb or a small word like to, for or with, use me, him, her, us or them.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses me, him, us or them before the verb.
misconceptions.cause: Uses the object form in a pair of names.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "___ went to the market." with "Me and Wanjiru" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Wanjiru and I", not "Me and Wanjiru".
misconceptions.feedback: Before a verb, who does the action? Use I, he, she, we or they: Wanjiru and I went to the market.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says the noun and then repeats it with a pronoun.
misconceptions.cause: Copies the pattern of speech where the name is said and then repeated.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Wanjiru ___ is tall." with "she" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "no pronoun", not "she".
misconceptions.feedback: Do not say the name and the pronoun together. Wanjiru is tall, or She is tall.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says he for a girl, or she for a boy.

example.question: Akinyi is my sister. ___ is nine.

misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili has one word (yeye) for he and she.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Akinyi is my sister. ___ is nine." with "He" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "She", not "He".
misconceptions.feedback: Use he for a boy or man and she for a girl or woman.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Writes my, your or her when no noun follows.
misconceptions.cause: Does not tell the two sets apart.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "That bag is ___." with "my" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "mine", not "my".
misconceptions.feedback: When no noun comes after, use mine, yours, hers, ours or theirs: That bag is mine.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes mine, yours or hers before a noun.
misconceptions.cause: Over-uses the form that stands alone.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "This is ___ pencil." with "mine" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "my", not "mine".
misconceptions.feedback: Before a noun use my, your, her, our or their: my pencil.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes your's, her's or our's.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks a belonging word needs an apostrophe, as in a name.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The blue pen is ___." with "your's" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "yours", not "your's".
misconceptions.feedback: Words like yours, hers, ours and theirs never have an apostrophe.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the possessive of another person.

example.question: Wafula, this book is not mine. It is ___.

misconceptions.cause: Does not follow who is speaking and who is spoken to.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Wafula, this book is not mine. It is ___." with "his" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "yours", not "his".
misconceptions.feedback: Ask who owns it. The person spoken to is you, so the word is yours.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Know the parts of a friendly letter
skills.mastery: Names and orders the parts of a friendly letter (address, date, greeting, body, closing, name) and the punctuation of the greeting and closing, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up the parts of a letter.
misconceptions.cause: Does not know the names of the parts.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which part says "Dear Amina,"?" with "closing" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "greeting", not "closing".
misconceptions.feedback: The greeting comes first and starts with Dear. The closing comes at the end, for example Yours lovingly.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the parts of the letter in the wrong order.

example.question: Which comes first in a friendly letter?

misconceptions.cause: Does not know the usual order.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which comes first in a friendly letter?" with "the closing" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "your address and the date", not "the closing".
misconceptions.feedback: A friendly letter goes: your address, the date, the greeting, the body, the closing, your name.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves the comma out after the greeting or the closing.
misconceptions.cause: Writes the greeting as a plain word group.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is correct?" with "Dear Amina" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Dear Amina,", not "Dear Amina".
misconceptions.feedback: A comma follows the greeting (Dear Amina,) and the closing (Yours lovingly,).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the receiver's address at the top of a friendly letter.

example.question: Whose address goes at the top?

misconceptions.cause: Copies the pattern of a formal letter.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Whose address goes at the top?" with "the person getting the letter" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "the writer", not "the person getting the letter".
misconceptions.feedback: In a friendly letter, write your own address at the top. Do not write the receiver's address there.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use words about food and a balanced diet
skills.mastery: Uses the words of nutrition (protein, vitamins, carbohydrates, balanced diet, fibre, nutrients) in the right sentence, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Picks a food word that is near in meaning but wrong.
misconceptions.cause: Mixes up the food groups.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Beans and meat give us ___." with "carbohydrates" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "protein", not "carbohydrates".
misconceptions.feedback: Protein builds the body (beans, meat, eggs). Carbohydrates give energy (ugali, rice, bread).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up vitamins and fibre.

example.question: ___ help us stay healthy and are found in fruits.

misconceptions.cause: Treats all nutrients as one.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "___ help us stay healthy and are found in fruits." with "Fibre" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Vitamins", not "Fibre".
misconceptions.feedback: Vitamins keep the body healthy. Fibre helps food move through the body.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks a balanced diet is one food in a large amount.

example.question: A balanced diet has ___.
example.correct_answer: all the food groups in the right amounts

misconceptions.cause: Does not know the meaning of balanced.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "A balanced diet has ___." with "only ugali" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "all the food groups in the right amounts", not "only ugali".
misconceptions.feedback: A balanced diet has food from all the food groups in the right amounts.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Scan a text for a detail
skills.mastery: Finds a number, time, price or name by looking for the key word in the question, not by reading every word, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Picks another number from the text.
misconceptions.cause: Does not look for the key word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "How much is a ticket?" with "60 shillings" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "50 shillings", not "60 shillings".
misconceptions.feedback: Scan for the key word in the question (ticket) and read only that line.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Looks for the wrong key word.
misconceptions.cause: Uses a word that is not the key word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "When does the show start?" with "at 6 pm" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "at 4 pm", not "at 6 pm".
misconceptions.feedback: Choose the key word that matches the question, then read the line.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads the whole text to find one detail.

example.question: What is the name of the guide?
example.wrong_answer: a long answer from the whole text

misconceptions.cause: Does not scan.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "What is the name of the guide?" with "a long answer from the whole text" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Mr Otieno", not "a long answer from the whole text".
misconceptions.feedback: Look for a capital letter or a number. Skip the rest.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Find adjectives in a sentence
skills.mastery: Names the describing word that tells more about a noun (tall girl, red bus) and does not pick the noun, the verb or an adverb, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Put adjectives of size and shape in order
skills.mastery: Puts size before shape before the noun (a big round ball) and never puts the adjective after the noun as in Kiswahili, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Picks the noun as the describing word.
misconceptions.cause: Does not tell what the word does in the sentence.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The red bus stopped." with "bus" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "red", not "bus".
misconceptions.feedback: An adjective describes a noun. Ask which word tells more about the bus: red.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks the verb as the describing word.
misconceptions.cause: Takes any word that adds meaning as a describing word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The tall girl ran home." with "ran" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "tall", not "ran".
misconceptions.feedback: A verb tells what someone does. An adjective tells what someone or something is like.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks an adverb as the adjective.
misconceptions.cause: Does not separate describing a noun from describing a verb.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The small boy walked slowly." with "slowly" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "small", not "slowly".
misconceptions.feedback: Slowly tells how the boy walked, so it is an adverb. Small tells what the boy is like, so it is the adjective.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a, an or the as the adjective.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks any small word before a noun describes it.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Mama bought a sweet mango." with "a" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "sweet", not "a".
misconceptions.feedback: A, an and the point to a noun but do not describe it. Sweet describes the mango.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the shape before the size.
misconceptions.cause: No fixed order is known.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "She sat on a ___ stool." with "round big" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "big round", not "round big".
misconceptions.feedback: Size comes first, then shape: a big round stool.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the adjective after the noun.
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili puts the adjective after the noun.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Amina has a ___." with "ball big" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "big ball", not "ball big".
misconceptions.feedback: In English the describing word comes before the noun: a big ball.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Joins two adjectives with and or a comma.
misconceptions.cause: Copies the way two things are joined in speech.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "a ___ table" with "big and round" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "big round", not "big and round".
misconceptions.feedback: Two describing words before a noun need no and and no comma: a big round table.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Know the parts of a narrative composition
skills.mastery: Says what the title, beginning, middle and end of a narrative tell (characters and setting, the problem, what happens, how it ends), in 8 of 10 new items.

skills.name: Put sentences in order to make a paragraph
skills.mastery: Finds the topic sentence and puts four jumbled sentences in the order that makes a clear paragraph, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Puts the end of the story at the beginning.

example.question: Which part tells how the story ends?

misconceptions.cause: Does not know what each part does.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which part tells how the story ends?" with "the beginning" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "the end", not "the beginning".
misconceptions.feedback: The beginning introduces people and place, the middle tells what happens, and the end tells how it finishes.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up setting and characters.

example.question: Which tells where and when a story happens?

misconceptions.cause: Uses the two words as if they meant the same.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which tells where and when a story happens?" with "the characters" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "the setting", not "the characters".
misconceptions.feedback: Characters are the people or animals in the story. The setting is where and when it happens.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Places the problem at the end instead of the middle.

example.question: Where does the problem of a story usually come?

misconceptions.cause: Thinks a story needs the problem last.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Where does the problem of a story usually come?" with "at the end" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "in the middle", not "at the end".
misconceptions.feedback: The problem usually starts in the middle. The end tells how it was solved.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks the title tells the whole story.

example.question: What does a title do?
example.correct_answer: gives a short name to the story

misconceptions.cause: Does not know the purpose of a title.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "What does a title do?" with "tells the whole story" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "gives a short name to the story", not "tells the whole story".
misconceptions.feedback: A title is a short name that hints at the story. It does not tell all of it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the sentences in the reverse order.

example.question: Put the four sentences in order.

misconceptions.cause: Starts from the sentence that sounds like an ending.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Put the four sentences in order." with "D C B A" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "A B C D", not "D C B A".
misconceptions.feedback: Start with the sentence that introduces the topic and read forward.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Swaps two neighbouring sentences.

example.question: Put the four sentences in order.

misconceptions.cause: Does not check the sequence words (first, then, next).
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Put the four sentences in order." with "A C B D" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "A B C D", not "A C B D".
misconceptions.feedback: Look at words like first, then, next and finally to see the order.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a detail as the topic sentence.

example.question: Which is the topic sentence?
example.correct_answer: the sentence that tells what the paragraph is about

misconceptions.cause: Picks the first sentence the eye meets.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is the topic sentence?" with "a detail" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "the sentence that tells what the paragraph is about", not "a detail".
misconceptions.feedback: The topic sentence names what the whole paragraph is about. The other sentences give details.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use many, much, few and little
skills.mastery: Uses many and few with things you can count and much and little with things you cannot count, in statements and questions, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use some, any, a lot of and enough
skills.mastery: Uses some in positive sentences, any in questions and negatives, a lot of and enough before the noun, and does not put enough after the noun, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses much with things that can be counted.
misconceptions.cause: Treats many and much as the same word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "There are not ___ chairs." with "much" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "many", not "much".
misconceptions.feedback: Use many with things you can count (chairs, books). Use much with things you cannot count (water, sugar).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses many with things that cannot be counted.
misconceptions.cause: Over-corrects after learning many.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "There is not ___ water." with "many" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "much", not "many".
misconceptions.feedback: You cannot count water one by one, so use much, not many.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses few with something uncountable, or little with something countable.
misconceptions.cause: Does not link few and little to what is counted.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "We have ___ sugar left." with "few" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "little", not "few".
misconceptions.feedback: Few goes with things you can count: few eggs. Little goes with things you cannot count: little sugar.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses much in a plain positive statement.
misconceptions.cause: Does not know that much is mostly kept for questions and negatives.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "She has ___ friends." with "much" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "many (or a lot of)", not "much".
misconceptions.feedback: In a positive sentence we usually say a lot of or many: She has many friends.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses any in a positive sentence.
misconceptions.cause: Does not tell positive from negative sentences.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I have ___ sugar." with "any" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "some", not "any".
misconceptions.feedback: Use some in a positive sentence: I have some sugar. Use any in a question or after not: I do not have any sugar.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses some after not.
misconceptions.cause: Keeps one word for all sentences.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I do not have ___ money." with "some" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "any", not "some".
misconceptions.feedback: After not or in a question, use any: I do not have any money. Do you have any money?
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts enough after the noun.
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili puts "enough" (tosha) after the noun.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "We have ___ for everyone." with "food enough" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "enough food", not "food enough".
misconceptions.feedback: In English enough comes before the noun: enough food.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Writes a lot before the noun without of.
misconceptions.cause: Leaves out the small word of.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "There are ___ mangoes." with "a lot mangoes" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "a lot of mangoes", not "a lot mangoes".
misconceptions.feedback: A lot needs of before the noun: a lot of mangoes.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Swaps two neighbouring pictures.
misconceptions.cause: Does not check what must happen before what.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which order tells the story?" with "A, C, B, D" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "A, B, C, D", not "A, C, B, D".
misconceptions.feedback: Ask what has to happen first for the next picture to make sense.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Tells the picture in the present tense when the story is in the past.
misconceptions.cause: Writes what he sees now.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which sentence tells the picture?" with "Wafula picks a mango." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Wafula picked a mango.", not "Wafula picks a mango.".
misconceptions.feedback: A story written after the event uses the past tense: Wafula picked a mango.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a sentence that does not match the picture.

misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which sentence tells the picture?" with "She sold the fruit." among the options.

misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use the past tense in a dialogue
skills.mastery: Uses the regular (-ed) and irregular (went, ate, saw) past forms when the time is past, and uses the present forms for habits and facts, in short dialogues, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses the plain verb for something that happened already.
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili shows the past in the verb start (nilienda), so the time word seems enough.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Yesterday I ___ to the market." with "go" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "went", not "go".
misconceptions.feedback: When the time is past, the verb must show it: Yesterday I went to the market.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Adds -ed to an irregular verb.
misconceptions.cause: Uses the regular rule for every verb.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "She ___ rice for lunch. (eat)" with "eated" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "ate", not "eated".
misconceptions.feedback: Some verbs change inside: go, went; eat, ate; see, saw. They do not take -ed.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses did with a past form.
misconceptions.cause: Marks the past twice.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Did you ___ the film?" with "saw" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "see", not "saw".
misconceptions.feedback: After did the verb stays plain: Did you see the film?
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the past form for a fact or a habit.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks a story always needs the past.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The sun ___ in the east." with "rose" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "rises", not "rose".
misconceptions.feedback: For a fact or something that always happens, use the present: The sun rises in the east.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use was and were with -ing
skills.mastery: Writes was or were plus the -ing verb for an action that was going on at a time in the past, and does not use is or are, a past form or a bare verb, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out am, is or are.
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili says "anasoma" with no separate helping word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "She ___ reading now." with "reading" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "is reading", not "reading".
misconceptions.feedback: An action happening now needs am, is or are before the -ing word: She is reading.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong form of be.
misconceptions.cause: Does not match the helping word to the subject.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The children ___ playing." with "is" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "are", not "is".
misconceptions.feedback: Use am with I, is with one person or thing, and are with you, we, they and plural nouns.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the plain verb after is or are.
misconceptions.cause: Forgets that the verb takes -ing after the helping word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "He is ___ now." with "play" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "playing", not "play".
misconceptions.feedback: After am, is or are, the verb ends in -ing: He is playing.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells the -ing form wrongly.
misconceptions.cause: Does not drop the silent e or double the last consonant.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "She is ___ a cake." with "makeing" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "making", not "makeing".
misconceptions.feedback: Drop the silent e before -ing (make, making). For short words with one vowel, double the last letter (run, running).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses is or are for an action that was going on in the past.
misconceptions.cause: Does not follow the time words of the sentence.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "When I arrived, Mum ___ cooking." with "is" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "was", not "is".
misconceptions.feedback: For something that was going on in the past, use was or were: Mum was cooking.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up was and were.
misconceptions.cause: Does not match the helping word to the subject.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The boys ___ running." with "was" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "were", not "was".
misconceptions.feedback: Use was with I and one person or thing. Use were with you, we, they and plural nouns.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes was or were with the past form of the verb.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks the verb must also show the past.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "He was ___ his lunch." with "ate" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "eating", not "ate".
misconceptions.feedback: After was or were, the verb ends in -ing: He was eating his lunch.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the plain verb after was or were.
misconceptions.cause: Forgets the -ing ending.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "They were ___ football." with "play" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "playing", not "play".
misconceptions.feedback: After was or were, the main verb takes -ing: They were playing football.

example.correct_answer: My mother went to the market.

misconceptions.cause: Thinks important words need capitals.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is right? My Mother went to the Market." with "My Mother went to the Market." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "My mother went to the market.", not "My Mother went to the Market.".
misconceptions.feedback: Only the first word of a sentence, names and I take a capital. Mother and market are ordinary words.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the name of a person or place with a small letter.

example.question: Which is right? we live in nairobi.

misconceptions.cause: Does not see a name as special.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is right? we live in nairobi." with "We live in nairobi." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "We live in Nairobi.", not "We live in nairobi.".
misconceptions.feedback: Names of people, places and days begin with a capital letter: Nairobi, Wanjiru, Monday.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes I as a small letter.

example.question: Which is right? Today i played football.

misconceptions.cause: Types i in a phone message.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is right? Today i played football." with "Today i played football." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Today I played football.", not "Today i played football.".
misconceptions.feedback: The word I always takes a capital letter.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use words about the farm
skills.mastery: Uses the words of the farm (harvest, seedlings, fertiliser, livestock, plough, weeding) in the right sentence, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Picks a farm word that is near in meaning but wrong.

example.question: We ___ the maize when it is ripe.

misconceptions.cause: Mixes up the steps of farming.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "We ___ the maize when it is ripe." with "plant" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "harvest", not "plant".
misconceptions.feedback: Planting comes first. Harvesting is gathering the crop when it is ripe.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up livestock and crops.
misconceptions.cause: Treats all farm things as one group.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Cows, goats and sheep are ___." with "crops" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "livestock", not "crops".
misconceptions.feedback: Livestock are farm animals. Crops are plants grown for food.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks fertiliser is a pest killer.

example.question: ___ makes the soil richer so that crops grow well.

misconceptions.cause: Does not know the two products.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "___ makes the soil richer so that crops grow well." with "Pesticide" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Fertiliser", not "Pesticide".
misconceptions.feedback: Fertiliser feeds the soil. Pesticide kills pests.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher
