skills.name: Write short forms of verbs
skills.mastery: Writes the short form (don't, isn't, can't, I'm, she's, we'll) with the apostrophe where the letter is missing, and tells it's (it is) from its (belonging to it), in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Turn a positive statement into a negative one
skills.mastery: Makes a negative with do not, does not, did not, is not or cannot, keeps the verb plain after does and did, and does not use two negatives together, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the apostrophe.
misconceptions.cause: Does not know the apostrophe marks the missing letter.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I ___ like fish. (do not)" with "dont" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "don't", not "dont".
misconceptions.feedback: The apostrophe takes the place of the missing letter: do not becomes don't.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the apostrophe in the wrong place.
misconceptions.cause: Puts it between the two words instead of where the letter is missing.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "She ___ at home. (is not)" with "is'nt" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "isn't", not "is'nt".
misconceptions.feedback: The apostrophe goes where the letter was left out: is not becomes isn't, with the mark in place of the o.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes its for it is, or it's for belonging to it.
misconceptions.cause: Mixes up the two words that sound the same.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "___ raining today. (it is)" with "Its" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "It's", not "Its".
misconceptions.feedback: It's means it is. Its (no apostrophe) means belonging to it: The cat licked its paw.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Makes a short form that does not exist.
misconceptions.cause: Adds n't to every helping word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "We ___ go. (will not)" with "willn't" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "won't", not "willn't".
misconceptions.feedback: A few short forms change: will not is won't, can not is can't.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses two negative words together.
misconceptions.cause: Copies speech where two negatives add emphasis.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I do not have ___ pen." with "no" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "a", not "no".
misconceptions.feedback: In English one negative is enough: I do not have a pen, or I have no pen.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes not before the verb with no helping word.
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili puts a negative in the verb itself (hapendi).
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "She ___ like milk." with "not" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "does not", not "not".
misconceptions.feedback: In English use do not or does not before the verb: She does not like milk.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Keeps -s or -ed on the verb after does not or did not.
misconceptions.cause: Marks the verb twice.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "He does not ___ meat." with "eats" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "eat", not "eats".
misconceptions.feedback: After does not and did not, the verb stays plain: He does not eat meat.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses do not with am, is or are.
misconceptions.cause: Uses do not for every negative.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I ___ tired." with "do not" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "am not", not "do not".
misconceptions.feedback: With am, is and are, put not after the helping word: I am not tired.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

recite poems containing adverbs of manner, time and place,

listen to a story or poem read by the teacher or from audio recordings and respond to questions,

key_inquiry_questions: Where do you live?
How do you do your work?
When do we come to school?

Communication and Collaboration: This is manifested when the learner play games involving categorising different types of adverbs collaboratively.

skills.name: Use adverbs of manner, time and place
skills.mastery: Says whether an adverb tells how, when or where, uses the adverb form (quickly, well) after the verb, and does not use an adjective where the adverb belongs, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses an adjective after the verb where an adverb is needed.
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili uses the same word for both in many sentences.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "She sings ___." with "beautiful" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "beautifully", not "beautiful".
misconceptions.feedback: A word that tells how someone does something is an adverb. Many adverbs end in -ly: sings beautifully.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Gives the wrong kind to an adverb of time, place or manner.
misconceptions.cause: Does not ask the question the adverb answers.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which kind of adverb is "yesterday"?" with "manner" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "time", not "manner".
misconceptions.feedback: Manner answers how, time answers when, place answers where. Yesterday tells when.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses good where well is needed.
misconceptions.cause: Does not know that good is an adjective.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "He plays football ___." with "good" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "well", not "good".
misconceptions.feedback: Good describes a noun (a good player). Well tells how something is done (plays well).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -ly to fast, hard or late.
misconceptions.cause: Over-uses the -ly rule.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The bus goes ___." with "fastly" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "fast", not "fastly".
misconceptions.feedback: Fast, hard and late are adverbs already. We say runs fast and works hard.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use commas in a list
skills.mastery: Puts a comma between the items of a list (with and before the last), not after the last item and not between a person and what the person does, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use the question mark
skills.mastery: Ends an asking sentence with a question mark, and a telling sentence with a full stop, even when the sentence has a question word in it, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the commas in a list.

example.question: Which is right? Mama bought rice beans and maize.
example.wrong_answer: Mama bought rice beans and maize.
example.correct_answer: Mama bought rice, beans and maize.

misconceptions.cause: Reads the list as one run of words.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is right? Mama bought rice beans and maize." with "Mama bought rice beans and maize." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Mama bought rice, beans and maize.", not "Mama bought rice beans and maize.".
misconceptions.feedback: In a list, put a comma between the items. Use and before the last one.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts a comma after the last item.

example.question: Which is right? I like mangoes, oranges, and bananas,
example.correct_answer: I like mangoes, oranges and bananas.

misconceptions.cause: Thinks every item needs a comma after it.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is right? I like mangoes, oranges, and bananas," with "I like mangoes, oranges, bananas," among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "I like mangoes, oranges and bananas.", not "I like mangoes, oranges, bananas,".
misconceptions.feedback: The last item has no comma after it. Put and before it and end with a full stop.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts a comma between who and what they do.

example.question: Which is right? Wafula, kicked the ball.

misconceptions.cause: Uses a comma as a breathing mark.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is right? Wafula, kicked the ball." with "Wafula, kicked the ball." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Wafula kicked the ball.", not "Wafula, kicked the ball.".
misconceptions.feedback: Do not put a comma between a person and what the person did. A comma is not a pause mark.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses full stops between the items of a list.

example.question: Which is right? We saw lions. zebras. and giraffes.
example.wrong_answer: We saw lions. zebras. and giraffes.
example.correct_answer: We saw lions, zebras and giraffes.

misconceptions.cause: Does not know the comma has its own job in lists.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is right? We saw lions. zebras. and giraffes." with "We saw lions. zebras. and giraffes." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "We saw lions, zebras and giraffes.", not "We saw lions. zebras. and giraffes.".
misconceptions.feedback: A full stop ends a whole sentence. Items in one list are separated by commas.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Ends a question with a full stop.

example.question: Which is right? Where is the book.

misconceptions.cause: Reads the question aloud with a rising voice but writes the usual end mark.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is right? Where is the book." with "Where is the book." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Where is the book?", not "Where is the book.".
misconceptions.feedback: A question ends with a question mark.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Ends a statement with a question mark because it has a question word in it.

example.question: Which is right? I do not know where he lives?
example.wrong_answer: I do not know where he lives?
example.correct_answer: I do not know where he lives.

misconceptions.cause: Sees the word where and thinks a question mark is needed.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is right? I do not know where he lives?" with "I do not know where he lives?" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "I do not know where he lives.", not "I do not know where he lives?".
misconceptions.feedback: A sentence that tells something ends with a full stop, even if it has a word like where in it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Ends a question with a comma.

example.question: Which is right? Are you hungry,

misconceptions.cause: Does not know a comma cannot end a sentence.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is right? Are you hungry," with "Are you hungry," among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Are you hungry?", not "Are you hungry,".
misconceptions.feedback: A comma never ends a sentence. A question ends with a question mark.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves the end mark out.

example.question: Which is right? What is your name

misconceptions.cause: Forgets the mark in quick writing.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is right? What is your name" with "What is your name" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "What is your name?", not "What is your name".
misconceptions.feedback: Every sentence needs an end mark. A question needs a question mark.

skills.name: Use words about hygiene and sanitation

misconceptions.error: Picks a hygiene word that is near in meaning but wrong.

example.question: Washing your hands kills ___ that cause diseases.

misconceptions.cause: Mixes up words in the same topic.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Washing your hands kills ___ that cause diseases." with "rubbish" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "germs", not "rubbish".
misconceptions.feedback: Germs are tiny living things that can cause disease. Rubbish is waste.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks disinfect means to make something smell nice.

example.question: We ___ the toilet with a strong cleaner to kill germs.

misconceptions.cause: Does not know the meaning.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "We ___ the toilet with a strong cleaner to kill germs." with "perfume" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "disinfect", not "perfume".
misconceptions.feedback: To disinfect is to kill germs on a surface.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up latrine and drainage.

example.question: A ___ is a place to dispose of human waste.

misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Join ideas with and, but, because, so and or
skills.mastery: Chooses the joining word that matches the meaning of the two parts (addition, contrast, reason, result, choice) and uses one joining word between two ideas, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses but where the two parts agree.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks every joining word is but.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Ali likes tea ___ coffee." with "but" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "and", not "but".
misconceptions.feedback: Use and to add one idea to another. Use but when the two ideas go against each other.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Swaps because and so.

example.question: It was raining, ___ we stayed inside.

misconceptions.cause: Mixes up a reason with a result.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "It was raining, ___ we stayed inside." with "because" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "so", not "because".
misconceptions.feedback: Because gives the reason. So gives the result. The rain is the reason; staying inside is the result.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses and where the two ideas go against each other.

example.question: I wanted to play, ___ I was tired.

misconceptions.cause: Uses and as the all-purpose joining word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I wanted to play, ___ I was tired." with "and" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "but", not "and".
misconceptions.feedback: When the second idea goes against the first, use but, not and.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses and where there is a choice.
misconceptions.cause: Does not hear the choice.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Would you like tea ___ juice?" with "and" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "or", not "and".
misconceptions.feedback: To offer a choice use or. And joins two things that are both there.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses or where both things happen.
misconceptions.cause: Does not hear the choice in or.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Mama bought rice ___ beans." with "or" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "and", not "or".
misconceptions.feedback: Or shows a choice between two things. And joins two things that are both there.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses two joining words for one link.

example.question: Although it was late, ___ we went on.

misconceptions.cause: Copies the two-word pattern of speech.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Although it was late, ___ we went on." with "but" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "no joining word", not "but".
misconceptions.feedback: One joining word is enough between two ideas. Use although or but, not both.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Know the parts of a descriptive composition
skills.mastery: Says what the introduction, the description (using the senses) and the conclusion of a descriptive composition do, and tells a description from a story, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Writes what happened instead of what the thing is like.

example.question: Which sentence is part of a description of a market?
example.wrong_answer: Yesterday I went to the market and bought a hat.
example.correct_answer: The market is noisy and smells of fresh fruit.

misconceptions.cause: Confuses a description with a story.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which sentence is part of a description of a market?" with "Yesterday I went to the market and bought a hat." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "The market is noisy and smells of fresh fruit.", not "Yesterday I went to the market and bought a hat.".
misconceptions.feedback: A description tells what something looks, sounds, smells, feels or tastes like. A story tells what happened.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses only what can be seen.

example.question: Which sentence uses a sense other than sight?

misconceptions.cause: Thinks describing means describing how it looks.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which sentence uses a sense other than sight?" with "The market is big." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "The market smells of fresh fruit.", not "The market is big.".
misconceptions.feedback: Use all the senses: sight, hearing, smell, touch and taste.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up the introduction and the conclusion.

example.question: Which part names what you will describe?

misconceptions.cause: Does not know the parts.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which part names what you will describe?" with "the conclusion" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "the introduction", not "the conclusion".
misconceptions.feedback: The introduction says what you are going to describe. The conclusion ends with a feeling or a last thought.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Ask questions with who, what, where, when, why, how and whose

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses who for a thing and what for a person.
misconceptions.cause: Does not link the question word to the kind of answer.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "___ is your teacher?" with "What" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Who", not "What".
misconceptions.feedback: Who asks about a person. What asks about a thing.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses where for a time and when for a place.

example.question: ___ do we start? At nine o'clock.

misconceptions.cause: Does not listen to the answer.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "___ do we start? At nine o'clock." with "Where" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "When", not "Where".
misconceptions.feedback: When asks about time. Where asks about a place. Why asks for a reason.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Keeps the statement order in a question.
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili questions keep the same order with a question word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Where ___ going?" with "you are" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "are you", not "you are".
misconceptions.feedback: In a question the helping word goes before the subject: Where are you going?
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Adds do to a question that already has is, are or can.
misconceptions.cause: Adds do to every question.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "How ___ you?" with "do are" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "are", not "do are".
misconceptions.feedback: Use only one helping word. How are you? Where do you live?
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes who's for whose.
misconceptions.cause: Mixes up two words that sound the same.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "___ bag is this?" with "Who's" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Whose", not "Who's".
misconceptions.feedback: Whose asks who owns something. Who's means who is.

misconceptions.error: Spells the word as it sounds.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Picks an environment word that is near in meaning but wrong.

example.question: To ___ plastic is to make it into something new.

misconceptions.cause: Mixes up words in the same topic.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "To ___ plastic is to make it into something new." with "litter" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "recycle", not "litter".
misconceptions.feedback: To recycle is to make waste into something new. Litter is rubbish dropped in a public place.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks pollution is a kind of plant.

example.question: ___ is the dirt that harms air, water or soil.

misconceptions.cause: Does not know the word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "___ is the dirt that harms air, water or soil." with "Compost" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Pollution", not "Compost".
misconceptions.feedback: Pollution is dirt or poison that harms the air, water or soil.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks conserve means to use up.

example.question: We should ___ water, not waste it.

misconceptions.cause: Does not know the word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "We should ___ water, not waste it." with "pollute" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "conserve", not "pollute".
misconceptions.feedback: To conserve is to look after and use carefully.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Know proverbs and what they teach
skills.mastery: Says the lesson of a common proverb and finishes a proverb with its right word, and does not read it as only about the animals or things in it, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Reads a proverb as only about its animals or things.

example.question: Haste makes waste means:
example.correct_answer: doing a thing too fast can spoil it

misconceptions.cause: Takes the words at face value.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Haste makes waste means:" with "people who hurry waste water" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "doing a thing too fast can spoil it", not "people who hurry waste water".
misconceptions.feedback: A proverb is a short saying with a lesson. Ask what it teaches people.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives the opposite lesson.

example.question: Slow and steady wins the race means:
example.correct_answer: keep going carefully and you will succeed

misconceptions.cause: Does not read the whole proverb.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Slow and steady wins the race means:" with "be fast to win" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "keep going carefully and you will succeed", not "be fast to win".
misconceptions.feedback: Check the lesson against the proverb. The lesson of this one is patience.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a lesson that has nothing to do with the proverb.

example.question: A stitch in time saves nine means:
example.correct_answer: fix a small problem early to avoid a big one

misconceptions.cause: Guesses from one word.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "A stitch in time saves nine means:" with "sewing is hard" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "fix a small problem early to avoid a big one", not "sewing is hard".
misconceptions.feedback: The lesson must fit the idea of the whole proverb.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Finishes a proverb with a word that sounds right but is not.
misconceptions.cause: Remembers the idea and not the exact words.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Easy come, easy ___." with "stay" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "go", not "stay".
misconceptions.feedback: A proverb always has the same words. Say the whole saying aloud.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use have and has with the past participle
skills.mastery: Writes have or has plus the past participle (have eaten, has gone) for an action that has just finished or still matters, and does not use it with yesterday or last week, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use had with the past participle
skills.mastery: Writes had plus the past participle for the action that happened first when two past actions are told, and keeps the order of the two events right, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses the simple past form after have or has.
misconceptions.cause: Does not know the past participle of irregular verbs.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I have ___ my lunch." with "ate" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "eaten", not "ate".
misconceptions.feedback: After have or has use the past participle: have eaten, has gone, have seen.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes have and has.
misconceptions.cause: Does not match the helping word to the subject.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "She ___ finished her work." with "have" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "has", not "have".
misconceptions.feedback: Use has with he, she, it and one person or thing. Use have with I, you, we, they and plural nouns.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the plain verb after have or has.
misconceptions.cause: Leaves out the past participle ending.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "They have ___ home." with "go" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "gone", not "go".
misconceptions.feedback: After have or has the verb needs its past participle: gone, taken, written.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses have or has with yesterday, last week or an exact past time.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks have or has is simply a past marker.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I ___ him yesterday." with "have seen" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "saw", not "have seen".
misconceptions.feedback: When the time is named (yesterday, last week), use the simple past: I saw him yesterday.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the simple past for both events.

example.question: The bus ___ left before I arrived.

misconceptions.cause: Does not mark which event came first.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The bus ___ left before I arrived." with "was" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "had", not "was".
misconceptions.feedback: The earlier of two past events takes had + participle: The bus had left before I arrived.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses have or has where had is needed.

example.question: When I got home, Mum ___ cooked.

misconceptions.cause: Does not move the helping word into the past.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "When I got home, Mum ___ cooked." with "has" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "had", not "has".
misconceptions.feedback: In a story about the past, use had, not have or has.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the plain verb after had.
misconceptions.cause: Forgets the past participle.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "She had ___ her homework." with "finish" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "finished", not "finish".
misconceptions.feedback: After had the verb is a participle: had finished, had gone.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts had on the event that happened second.

example.question: Which happened first? Wanjiru had left when I arrived.

misconceptions.cause: Does not see that had marks the earlier event.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which happened first? Wanjiru had left when I arrived." with "I arrived" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Wanjiru left", not "I arrived".
misconceptions.feedback: The event with had happened first. Wanjiru had left, then I arrived.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

learning_experiences: identify components of a diary individually,
view samples of diaries and discuss them with peers,
search for information on how to write personal diaries from electronic devices or printed sources,
write a diary with peers and display it to the rest of the class members.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we keep a record of what we do?
What information do we record?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: These competencies are manifested when the learner comes up with their own diary and displays it for the rest of the class members.
Digital Literacy: This is achieved as learner ably manipulates digital devices when searching for information on how to write a diary from electronic resources.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: This is inculcated as the learner applies their diary in their day-to-day operations.
sub_strands.pcis: Self-esteem: The learner’s self-esteem is enhanced as they search for information on how to write a diary and apply it in their writing of a diary.
sub_strands.links: The learner applies the knowledge of writing a diary to learning of the same concept in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify the components of a diary for effective writing
write a diary in the right format for effective communication
adopt the use of diaries in our day-today lives

skills.name: Know the parts of a diary entry
skills.mastery: Says what a diary entry has (date, a greeting to the diary, what happened and how the writer felt, in the first person and the past tense) and what it does not have, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Leaves the date out.

example.question: What does every diary entry start with?

misconceptions.cause: Thinks the diary is only for reading by the writer.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "What does every diary entry start with?" with "a title" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "the date", not "a title".
misconceptions.feedback: A diary entry begins with the date, so you know when it happened.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the diary as a letter to a person.

example.question: Which is the best start of a diary entry?

misconceptions.cause: Mixes up the friendly letter and the diary.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which is the best start of a diary entry?" with "Dear Mum, how are you?" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "Monday, 4th March. Dear Diary,", not "Dear Mum, how are you?".
misconceptions.feedback: A diary is written to yourself. Begin with the date and Dear Diary, not Dear Mum.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes about himself or herself as he or she.

example.question: Which sentence is in the right voice?

misconceptions.cause: Writes as in a story told by someone else.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which sentence is in the right voice?" with "Wanjiru woke up early." among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "I woke up early.", not "Wanjiru woke up early.".
misconceptions.feedback: A diary is about you, so write in the first person: I woke up early.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes only a list of events, with no feelings.

example.question: What else does a diary entry have besides what happened?

misconceptions.cause: Thinks a diary is a record only.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "What else does a diary entry have besides what happened?" with "a list of names" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "how the writer felt", not "a list of names".
misconceptions.feedback: A diary also tells how you felt: I was happy when we won.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

learning_experiences: identify the sounds /k/ in letter x as well as the sounds /m/ /n/ /ŋ// from an oral text,

listen to stories related to the theme from a teacher or audio recordings,
play the telephone game with peers,
make sentneces with the target language pattern ‘very...but...’.

skills.name: Use words about money
skills.mastery: Uses the words of money (savings, budget, price, change, loan, borrow, earn) in the right sentence and does not swap earn with save or borrow with lend, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Find the silent letter in a word
skills.mastery: Names the silent letter in words like knife, write, lamb, listen, hour and walk, and does not pick the letter beside it, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Swaps earn and save.

example.question: Mama ___ money every month to buy a cow later.

misconceptions.cause: Does not tell getting money from keeping it.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Mama ___ money every month to buy a cow later." with "earns" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "saves", not "earns".
misconceptions.feedback: To earn is to get money for work. To save is to keep money for later.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Swaps borrow and lend.

example.question: Can I ___ your pen? I will return it.

misconceptions.cause: Does not tell who takes and who gives.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Can I ___ your pen? I will return it." with "lend" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "borrow", not "lend".
misconceptions.feedback: You borrow when you take for a short time. You lend when you give for a short time.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a money word that is near in meaning but wrong.

example.question: A ___ helps a family plan how to spend its money.

misconceptions.cause: Mixes up words in the same topic.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "A ___ helps a family plan how to spend its money." with "price" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "budget", not "price".
misconceptions.feedback: Read the whole sentence and say what the gap must mean before you choose.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up price and change.

example.question: The ___ of the book is 80 shillings.

misconceptions.cause: Treats the money words as the same.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The ___ of the book is 80 shillings." with "change" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "price", not "change".
misconceptions.feedback: The price is what something costs. Change is the money given back.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks the letter beside the silent one.
misconceptions.cause: Does not say the word slowly.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which letter is silent in "knife"?" with "n" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "k", not "n".
misconceptions.feedback: Say the word aloud. In knife you hear n, but not k.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks every letter is sounded.
misconceptions.cause: Does not know silent letters.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which letter is silent in "write"?" with "none" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "w", not "none".
misconceptions.feedback: Some letters are written but not said. In write, the w is silent.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks the silent letter is always the last letter.
misconceptions.cause: Has learnt silent e at the end.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Which letter is silent in "lamb"?" with "m" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "b", not "m".
misconceptions.feedback: A silent letter can be anywhere. In lamb the b is silent.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use in, on, under, behind, between and next to
skills.mastery: Chooses the preposition that says where a thing is (in, on, under, behind, in front of, between, next to) from the picture in words, in 8 of 10 new sentences, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use to, into, out of, across, through and along
skills.mastery: Chooses the preposition that says where something moves (into the room, out of the house, across the road, through the gate), and does not write to home or go at school, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up in and on.
misconceptions.cause: Does not picture the position.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The cup is ___ the table." with "in" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "on", not "in".
misconceptions.feedback: On means touching the top of something. In means inside it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses between for three or more things, or among for two.

example.question: The ball is ___ the two boys.

misconceptions.cause: Does not count the things.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The ball is ___ the two boys." with "among" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "between", not "among".
misconceptions.feedback: Use between for two things and among for more than two.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks the opposite preposition.

example.question: The cat is ___ the bed (hiding below it).

misconceptions.cause: Does not picture where the thing is.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The cat is ___ the bed (hiding below it)." with "on" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "under", not "on".
misconceptions.feedback: Under means below something. Behind means at the back of it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up in front of and behind.

example.question: Juma stood ___ Achieng at the end of the line.

misconceptions.cause: Does not picture the line.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Juma stood ___ Achieng at the end of the line." with "in front of" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "behind", not "in front of".
misconceptions.feedback: In front of means before it. Behind means after it, at the back.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses to where into (going inside) is needed.
misconceptions.cause: Does not feel the idea of going inside.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "He ran ___ the room." with "to" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "into", not "to".
misconceptions.feedback: Into shows going from outside to inside a place. To shows going towards it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses at after go.
misconceptions.cause: Mixes the place and the movement words.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "We go ___ school every day." with "at" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "to", not "at".
misconceptions.feedback: After go use to: go to school. At tells where something is.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Writes to before home.
misconceptions.cause: Copies the pattern "go to school".
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I went ___ after school." with "to home" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "home", not "to home".
misconceptions.feedback: Home needs no word before it after go: I went home.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes through and across.

example.question: The goat ran ___ the road to the other side.

misconceptions.cause: Does not picture the movement.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The goat ran ___ the road to the other side." with "through" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "across", not "through".
misconceptions.feedback: Across means from one side of a flat place to the other. Through means passing in at one side and out at the other.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.core_competences:
Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: The learner forms words with double consonants from jumbled up letters.
Learning to Learn: This is encouraged as the learner learns how to spell words through learner centred activities such as peer dictation, jigsaw puzzles and watching video as they write words learnt from peers.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: It is portrayed as the learner takes turns while watching a video with peers and also shares the resources amicably to watch videos.
Integrity: This is achieved as the learner displays self-discipline and honesty when watching videos online and writing down words with double consonants used in the video.
sub_strands.pcis:
Effective Communication: This is enhanced as the learner learns how to spell words correctly thereby effectively communicating especially in written form.
Financial Literacy: The learner listens to audio recordings and watches videos about the theme of money to pick out words on double consonants.
sub_strands.links: The learner ably transfers the knowledge on proper spelling to all other learning areas as they all emphasise on correct spelling in written work.

skills.name: Spell words with double consonants
skills.mastery: Spells words with a double consonant (summer, coffee, address, rabbit, letter) and does not double a letter that has only one, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Writes one consonant where there are two.
misconceptions.cause: Does not hear the two letters.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "Mama drinks ___ every morning." with "cofee" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "coffee", not "cofee".
misconceptions.feedback: Some words have two of the same letter together: coffee, summer, letter.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells the word as it sounds.
misconceptions.cause: Writes what the ear hears and picks a wrong vowel.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "The ___ ran into its hole." with "rabbet" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "rabbit", not "rabbet".
misconceptions.feedback: Say the word slowly and then check it. Rabbit has bb in the middle.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Doubles a letter that is single.

example.question: I wrote a ___ to my aunt.

misconceptions.cause: Over-corrects after learning double letters.
misconceptions.reveals: A question like "I wrote a ___ to my aunt." with "lettter" among the options.
misconceptions.help: Have the child say both forms aloud and say why one fits: "letter", not "lettter".
misconceptions.feedback: Only some letters are doubled. Check each word: letter has tt but not three t.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher
